summary: Explains that the RFC 2544 benchmarking methods are meant for isolated lab testing and should not be run on production networks. They deliberately overload device resources, which would likely harm real user traffic. It clarifies the intended scope of RFC 2544. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A test that pushes a machine until it nearly breaks is fine in a workshop. This says do not do it on the busy road where real people are driving.

questions: can rfc 2544 be used on production networks
why is rfc 2544 only for lab testing
what is an isolated test environment
what is the rfc 2544 throughput test
subtitle: Why the RFC 2544 benchmarking tests belong in the lab and must not be run on live networks.

tldr.problem: RFC 2544 benchmarking methods were being used to check live services, such as SLAs and service activation, where they were never meant to be used.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement limits RFC 2544 to an isolated test environment, explains how the tests overload devices and give flawed results elsewhere, and points to other work for production measurement.
tldr.outcome: It says the RFC 2544 tests MUST NOT be used on production networks, and it updates RFC 2544 to make that scope clear.

today: RFC 6815 is an Informational RFC published in November 2012, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2544 by stating that its tests are for isolated test environments only.

sections.title: The Problem Being Addressed
sections.content:
This memo clarifies the scope of the benchmarking tests of the IETF Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG), starting with RFC 2544. Those tests rely on conditions that can only be produced and replicated reliably in a laboratory.

The RFC lists uses it considers inappropriate: validating a Committed Information Rate (CIR), validating metrics in a Service Level Agreement (SLA) such as frame loss and latency, and service activation testing, where traffic sharing network resources with the test might be adversely affected.

The authors also note that the methods actually used in the field vary from RFC 2544 in significant ways. Because the only citation is RFC 2544, those changes are opaque to the standards community.
sections.plainLanguage: People were using a lab test on real networks, like using a crash test on a car that is already on the highway. This memo says that was never the plan.

sections.title: The Isolated Test Environment
sections.content:
The memo's goal is to limit RFC 2544 to laboratory testing. The setting it assumes is an Isolated Test Environment (ITE), which can contain the test streams to paths within the desired setup and prevent non-test traffic from traversing the test setup.

This lets testers experiment freely while protecting lab management and control LANs and other production networks from the effects of the test traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: An isolated test environment is a closed test track. Nothing gets in, and nothing gets out.

sections.title: Why the Tests Only Fit the Lab
sections.content:
There are two reasons. The first is experimental control and accuracy. Every RFC 2544 test requires that the tester and the device under test are the only devices transmitting data. Other traffic means the specified conditions are not met, and results become hard to repeat. The Throughput Test deliberately goes above the maximum load that causes frame loss, so any extra traffic causes loss at a lower tester rate than would otherwise be seen.

The second is containing damage. The methods may overload the device under test and cause failure modes in it. They can also hurt traffic that shares resources with the test, since the load is usually close to link capacity.

RFC 2544 assigns the address range 198.18.0.0 through 198.19.255.255 to the BMWG for testing. Internet devices may discard traffic in that range, so test packets forwarded across the Internet will likely be dropped and the test will not work. The memo also notes an IPv6 range assigned to BMWG for laboratory use in RFC 5180.
sections.plainLanguage: The test needs an empty room to give a fair answer, and it can knock things over if other people are in the room.

sections.title: The Advisory for Production Networks
sections.content:
The RFC 2544 tests were designed to measure network devices, not networks, and certainly not production networks carrying user traffic. One problem is that the methods treat frame loss as the sign of resource exhaustion. Real networks suffer link-layer and physical-layer errors, so they do not run loss-free, and Throughput will not be assessed correctly. Flawed results waste time for the user of the testing service and for the provider who must dispute them.

The memo is blunt: the tests MUST NOT be used on production networks. It adds that the methods have never been validated on a network path, even one that is not part of a production network and carries no other traffic, so such use is contraindicated by the BMWG.

Appendix A walks through the Throughput method: raise the offered load step by step, count the frames received, and report the highest rate with no loss. Because loss is the only signal, random loss from optical or electrical interference on a long production path makes the reported Throughput falsely low.
sections.plainLanguage: On a real road there are always bumps and potholes. The test mistakes every bump for the car being too full, so it gives the wrong answer.

sections.title: Security and Where to Go Instead
sections.content:
Section 6 points readers elsewhere. The IETF chartered the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group to standardize metrics for production networks, though some IPPM metrics differ from RFC 2544 metrics with similar names. IPPM has not yet standardized methods for raw capacity measurement of Internet paths. The memo also mentions the ITU-T Recommendation Y.1564 on service activation test methodology, and encourages people who need capacity tests on production networks to take part in standards work.

For security, the memo says that limiting benchmarking to a laboratory avoids accidental denial-of-service attacks or congestion from high-volume test streams. The test topology MUST NOT be connected to devices that may forward test traffic into a production network. Benchmarking is black-box, and special benchmarking capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the device under test.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need to test the real road, use a different, gentler tool that people are still building. Until then, keep the crash tests in the lab.
